introBasis: your Auto Engineering and DreamControl results, and the setup questions robot buyers ask before they commit
offerText: Your first article is on me.

cards.title: Robot Onboarding: The Month Nobody Budgets
cards.angle: Physical Intelligence hit an $11B valuation in March 2026 and NVIDIA is recruiting toward 2 million robotics developers, yet buyers still lose weeks per robot before any policy runs. The bottleneck is the integration layer, not the model.
cards.evidence: Your September 2026 Auto Engineering post shows a first Flexiv Rizon skill in about four hours (20 minutes ingestion, 10 minutes sim, the rest skill creation) and later skills in 10 to 15 minutes, against the month-long baseline your CEO gave GeekWire. No article on your site walks a buyer through where those four hours go.
cards.formatNote: One first-party log and one market shift.

cards.title: Sim-to-Real Fails in Millimetres, Not Models
cards.angle: NVIDIA shipped Cosmos world models at CES 2026 to flood robots with synthetic data, and the field still treats transfer as a model-quality problem. Your own log says calibration and timing decide it first.
cards.evidence: Your Auto Engineering post reports a system-identification error cut from 143 mm and 6.4 degrees to 5.7 mm and 0.68 degrees, a depth-plane error cut from 28.0 mm to 1.2 mm, and a controller pacing at 500 Hz where the arm expected 30 Hz. Those are the most concrete transfer numbers any vendor published this year and they sit inside a launch post.
cards.formatNote: One set of measured errors against one industry assumption.

cards.title: One Human Video: What Teleop Still Costs
cards.angle: Generalist raised $200M at $3B in August 2026 on learning tasks from short human videos, while Western teleop labor runs $25 to $48 an hour and a task still eats dozens of demonstrations. The question is not whether video replaces teleop but what the residual correction loop costs per episode.
cards.evidence: Your pipeline turns a single human video into simulated robot experience through hand-pose estimation and Gaussian-splat reconstruction, then fine-tunes with behavior cloning and DAgger, with GELLO arms for corrections. You have never priced the correction step publicly, and that is the number a buyer comparing you to a data vendor wants.
cards.formatNote: A cost breakdown the buyer compares against data vendors across several factors.

cards.title: Humanoid Control: Where the Small Policy Starts
cards.angle: Figure 03 entered BMW Spartanburg in June 2026 and Physical Intelligence's 3 to 5B parameter model needs about 100 ms to plan 50 steps. Below that a fast reflex policy has to take over, and nobody has drawn the boundary in public.
cards.evidence: Your DreamControl work (ICRA 2026) runs whole-body drawer, lift and locomotion skills on a Unitree G1 with a control policy under 1 million parameters, guided by a diffusion prior on human motion. The post explains the method and never argues the architecture question it answers.
cards.formatNote: One position, argued in the founder's voice.

cards.title: Fifty OEMs, One Interface: Fragmentation as the Product
cards.angle: Accenture Ventures invested in April 2026 to push physical AI into manufacturing and logistics, where a single plant runs arms, quadrupeds and AMRs from different vendors. Your CEO's stated constraint is the lack of unified intelligence infrastructure, not a shortage of models.
cards.evidence: Your GRID page lists 17 supported OEMs including Boston Dynamics, Unitree, Kinova, FANUC and ANYbotics, and the September 2026 post claims 50+ integrated. What an integration actually requires per OEM (drivers, kinematics, safety interlocks, sim twin) is undocumented, and it is the buyer's first due-diligence question.
cards.formatNote: A buyer's due-diligence guide, compared OEM by OEM across several factors.
